A study involving 119 participants, rated as having a low risk of bias, compared a combination treatment (aerobic and core strengthening exercises combined with graded activity and problem-solving training) to graded activity with problem-solving training alone. The study did not report follow-up scores but provided within-group mean changes. 2. Dalichau (2003) was excluded from the meta-analysis due to missing data. This study, involving 90 participants and rated as having a high risk of bias, compared mixed exercise to no or no additional treatment. The authors reported greater disability improvement in the exercise group, although the effect estimates were unclear. 3. McIlveen (1998) was excluded from the meta-analysis due to missing data. This study, involving 95 participants and rated as having a high risk of bias, reported outcomes using the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) on a 0–100 scale. 4. Kanwal (2021), involving 24 participants and rated as having a high risk of bias, compared core strengthening exercises to no or no additional treatment. This study was excluded from the meta-analysis due to missing data. 5. Raza (2020), involving 40 participants and rated as having a high risk of bias, examined stretching or flexibility/mobilizing exercises. No significant differences were found for individual ODI items (0–5 scale). 6. Da Silva (2014), involving 18 participants and rated as having a high risk of bias, investigated mixed exercise interventions. The study reported benefits indicated by lower scores on the Roland-Morris Disability Questionnaire (RMDQ, 0–24 scale). 7. Wattamwar (2012), involving 24 participants and rated as having a high risk of bias, studied yoga exercises. This study was excluded from the meta-analysis due to missing data. 8. Sedaghati (2017), involving 34 participants and rated as having a high risk of bias, compared mixed exercises (in and out of water) and stretching or flexibility/mobilizing exercises. 9. Liu (2018), involving 43 participants and rated as having a high risk of bias, studied Tai Chi and core strengthening exercises. The authors reported significant decreases in average ODI scores in both exercise groups compared to the comparison group, although overall scores were not reported (ODI 0–50 scale). 10. Rathi (2013), involving 30 participants and rated as having a high risk of bias, investigated core strengthening exercises. Benefits were indicated by lower ODI scores (0–100 scale). 11. Several studies reported inconsistencies in their findings, with overlapping confidence intervals and high heterogeneity (I² values ranging from 63% to 97%). These inconsistencies could not be fully explained by small subgroup sizes and may represent substantial heterogeneity. 12. Smeets (2008), involving 119 participants and rated as having a low risk of bias, compared a combination of physical training and graded activity with problem-solving training to graded activity with problem-solving training alone. This study was excluded from the meta-analysis due to missing follow-up scores. 13. Numerous other studies explored various interventions for chronic low back pain, including aquatic exercise, stabilization exercises, virtual reality training, yoga, Tai Chi, Pilates, neuromuscular electrical stimulation, and mindfulness-based approaches. These studies often reported improvements in pain, disability, and quality of life, although many were excluded from meta-analyses due to missing data or high risk of bias. 14. The WHO guideline on the non-surgical management of chronic primary low back pain in adults summarized evidence from these studies, emphasizing the importance of individualized and evidence-based approaches to treatment. This summary reflects the detailed findings and limitations of the studies, highlighting the diversity of interventions and the challenges in synthesizing evidence due to methodological inconsistencies and missing data.
